opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that each of these data sources has always had a fatal flaw on its own, and what's changed is that they now cover for each other's weaknesses.

Take simulation. For years the problem was the sim-to-real gap. You could train a policy that looked beautiful in sim, and the moment it touched a real object with real friction and real lighting, it fell apart. Simulation is still imperfect, but it's gotten much better at being diverse. You can randomize physics, textures, and object geometry at a scale you could never collect in the real world. For things like locomotion, and increasingly for some dexterous skills, that diversity matters more than perfect fidelity.

Then there's human-generated data, whether that's teleoperation or people wearing cameras doing everyday tasks. Teleop gives you very high quality, on-embodiment data, but it's expensive and slow. You're bottlenecked by how many operators and robots you have. Egocentric human video is the opposite. It's cheap and abundant, and it captures the long tail of how people actually manipulate the world, but the embodiment is wrong. A human hand isn't a parallel gripper. What's exciting is that we're getting better at retargeting, and at learning representations where the "what to do" transfers even if the "how to move the joints" doesn't.

Video models are maybe the newest piece and the one I'm most excited about. These models have absorbed an enormous amount of implicit physics and common sense from internet-scale video. They know that a cup tipped over spills, and that a drawer slides along one axis. If you can use that as a prior, as a world model for planning, as a source of synthetic training data, or as a way to evaluate policies without running them on hardware, you're getting knowledge about the world that no robot fleet could collect.

So the optimism comes from the combination. Video models give you broad semantic and physical priors. Human data gives you realistic behavior and task structure. Simulation gives you scale and safe exploration, especially for reinforcement learning. A comparatively small amount of real robot data then grounds all of it in the actual embodiment. That's a much more data-efficient recipe than "just collect a million hours of teleop," which is basically where the field was a few years ago.

I'll add one caveat, because I don't want to oversell it. We don't yet have a clean recipe for how to weight and mix these sources, and evaluation in robotics is still really hard. But the trajectory feels a lot like the early days of language models. Once you have a scalable way to get diverse data, progress tends to compound. For the first time, I think robotics has a plausible path to that kind of scaling.

r001.rationale: The response describes video models, human data, and simulation as complementary sources, but does not identify video models as a point where human-generated data and simulation converge.

r002.rationale: The response mentions video models as priors and a source of synthetic training data, but does not say video-generated environments need physics-simulation grounding for physical realism.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that none of these three sources is sufficient on its own, and for a long time the field kind of treated them as competing bets rather than complementary ones. What's changed for me is that the weaknesses of each one are now pretty well understood, and they happen to line up in a way where each one covers the others' gaps.

Take human-generated data first. When we did things like RT-1 and RT-2, the real teleoperation data was the backbone. It's grounded, it's physically correct, the contact dynamics are real, and it captures the kind of messy real-world variation you just can't script. But it's brutally expensive. You're talking about operators standing at robots for months, and even then you end up with maybe a hundred thousand episodes, which by language model standards is nothing. So the scaling story was always the problem. You can see the curves bending upward, but you can't afford to ride them very far.

Simulation is the obvious answer to the scaling problem, and the reason I wasn't that optimistic about it five years ago is that the sim-to-real gap was genuinely bad. Physics engines were fine for rigid bodies and terrible for anything deformable or with complex contact, and visually it looked like a video game. What's changed is partly that the engines got better, but mostly that the representations the policies are learning on have gotten so much more robust. If your policy is operating on top of a vision backbone that's seen billions of real images, a slightly off rendering is much less catastrophic than it used to be. The gap didn't close so much as the model learned to be indifferent to it.

And then video models are the piece that I think a lot of people are still underrating. The thing a video model gives you is an implicit physics model learned from an enormous amount of human footage. It knows what happens when you push a cup toward the edge of a table. It knows roughly how a towel folds. It doesn't know it precisely, and it will hallucinate, but it has a prior about the world that is dramatically richer than anything you'd hand-write into a simulator. So you can use it in a few ways. You can use it to generate plausible trajectories or subgoals, you can use it as a kind of learned world model to plan against, and you can use it to augment the small amount of real data you have into much more diverse training signal.

So the way I think about it now is almost like a stack. Human data is the ground truth anchor that keeps you honest about what real physics actually does. Simulation is where you get volume and controlled variation, where you can deliberately generate the long-tail situations you'd never see in a teleop session. And video models are the glue that brings in a general understanding of how the world behaves, which is the thing neither of the other two gives you.

The reason I'm optimistic specifically now, rather than in principle, is that we've got enough evidence from language that this recipe works. Pretraining on a broad, somewhat noisy, enormous corpus, then grounding it with a smaller amount of high-quality targeted data. Robotics never had the enormous corpus. Video and sim are how we're finally getting one. And when I look at the results coming out, the ones that excite me are not the ones where someone trained a single-task policy really well. They're the ones where a model trained on one embodiment with mostly generated data transfers to a new task on a new robot with a handful of real demonstrations. That's the signal that the generalization story is starting to work, and it's exactly what you'd predict if the three data sources are actually compounding.

r001.rationale: The response describes the three sources as complementary and calls video models “the glue” for general world understanding, but does not identify video models as a convergence point between human-generated data and simulation.

r002.rationale: The response discusses simulation and video models separately; it does not say video-generated environments need grounding in physics simulation for physical realism.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting thing is that these sources of data are complementary. Simulation gives you a place to practice, to try things repeatedly, and to get feedback without putting a real robot at risk. Human demonstrations give you examples of what useful behavior looks like. And video gives you access to a much broader range of interactions with the world than we could ever collect with robots alone.

The challenge is that none of those is sufficient by itself. A video doesn’t tell you exactly what forces were applied, and a policy that works in simulation may still fail in the real world. But you can imagine using video to learn representations and expectations about how the world changes, human data to guide the behavior, and simulation to practice and refine it. Then real robot experience helps ground all of that.

So my optimism comes from having more ways to learn than just collecting every experience on a physical robot. There are still hard questions about how to combine these signals, but they give us a much richer starting point.

sol-6.1.text:
I think what’s exciting is that these sources of data have complementary strengths. Simulation gives us scale and control: we can vary environments, repeat experiments, and generate situations that would be difficult to collect on a real robot. Human-generated data gives us examples of useful behavior and how people interact with the world. And video models offer a way to learn more about how the world changes over time from a much broader range of experience.

The opportunity is to bring those together, rather than expect any one of them to solve robotics on its own. A robot needs to understand what might happen, but it also needs to know what actions it can take to make something happen. Watching a video isn’t the same as learning that connection, and simulation still has gaps relative to the real world.

But we have increasingly useful ways to combine those ingredients and then ground them in real robot experience. That makes me optimistic: we can potentially get much more learning out of every interaction, instead of collecting every skill from scratch on hardware.

r001.rationale: It says human-generated data, simulation, and video models can be combined, but does not identify video models as a point of convergence between the other two.

r002.rationale: It notes that simulation has gaps relative to the real world and that learning should be grounded in real robot experience, but does not say video-generated environments need grounding in physics simulation for physical realism.
